bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- High customer concentration: Top 10 customers contributed 72.14% of Revenue from Operations in Fiscal 2026. — Loss of any major customer, particularly government/PSU clients, could significantly impact revenue and cash flows.
- Tender-based business model with government counterparties. — Revenue depends on winning competitive bids; contracts with government entities entail long credit periods, creating working capital strain and payment uncertainty.
- Geographic concentration in East India. — Operations and manufacturing are concentrated in West Bengal; execution in difficult terrains (forests, flood zones) increases cost and complexity.
- Working capital intensity. — EPC projects and government contracts typically have long gestation and payment cycles, potentially pressuring liquidity and requiring sustained borrowing.
- Raw material price volatility (aluminium, copper, PVC). — Primary inputs are commodities with fluctuating prices; inability to pass on cost increases could compress margins.
- Execution risk in new high-voltage EPC segment. — Expansion into 66 kV+ transmission EPC involves larger, more complex projects; delays or cost overruns could adversely affect financials.

compliance_legal.detail: SEBI and the Stock Exchanges, in the past, have introduced various pre-emptive surveillance measures with respect to the shares of listed companies in India in order to enhance market integrity, safeguard the interests of investors and potential market abuses. compliance_legal.detail: We are incorporated under the laws of India and most of our Directors, Key Managerial Personnel and Senior Management reside in India. As of the date of this Red Herring Prospectus, all of our assets are located in India. Where investors wish to enforce foreign judgments in India, they may face difficulties in enforcing such judgments. India exercises reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters with a limited number of jurisdictions. In order to be enforceable, a judgment obtained in a jurisdiction which India recognizes as a reciprocating territory must meet certain requirements of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
compliance_legal.evidence: India is not a party to any international treaty in relation to the recognition or enforcement of foreign judgments. Section 44A of the CPC provides that where a certified copy of a decree of any superior court obtained in any country or territory outside India which the government has by notification declared to be in a reciprocating territory, may be enforced in India by proceedings in execution as if the judgment had been rendered by a district court in India. However, Section 44A of the CPC is applicable only to monetary decrees and does not apply to decrees for amounts payable in respect of taxes, other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalties and does not apply to arbitration awards. The United States has not been declared by the GoI to be a reciprocating territory for the purposes of Section 44A of the CPC. The suit must be brought in India within three years from the date of judgment.
compliance_legal.title: Investors may not be able to enforce a judgment of a foreign court against us, our Directors, and executive officers in India respectively, except by way of a law suit in India

financial_valuation.detail: Under current Indian tax laws, unless specifically exempted, capital gains arising from the sale of equity shares held as investments in an Indian company are generally taxable in India. Any capital gain realized on the sale of listed equity shares on a Stock Exchange held for more than 12 months immediately preceding the date of transfer will be subject to long-term capital gains tax in India at the specified rates. STT will be levied on and collected by a domestic stock exchange on which the Equity Shares are sold. Further, any capital gains realized on the sale of listed equity shares held for a period of 12 months or less immediately preceding the date of transfer will be subject to short-term capital gains tax in India.
financial_valuation.evidence: In terms of the Finance Act, with effect from July 24, 2024, taxes payable by an assessee on the capital gains arising from transfer of long-term capital assets (introduced as Section 112A of the Income-Tax Act, 1961) shall be calculated on such long-term capital gains at the rate of 12.5%, where the long-term capital gains exceed ₹125,000. The stamp duty for transfer of certain securities, other than debentures, on a delivery basis is currently specified at 0.015% and on a non-delivery basis is specified at 0.003% of the consideration amount.
financial_valuation.title: Investors may be subject to Indian taxes arising out of capital gains on the sale of the Equity Shares

parameter_scores.basis: Integrated manufacturing + EPC model with backward integration provides cost advantages, but heavy dependence on power infrastructure sector, government budgetary allocations, and top 10 customers (72.14% of revenue in FY26) creates vulnerability. Manufacturing segment alone contributed 72.70% of revenue in FY26. Capacity utilization declining to 61.59% despite capacity expansion signals demand-supply mismatch risk.

Total borrowings ₹8,282.34 million (FY26) with finance costs ₹1,331.06 million; interest coverage ratio 2.21x (FY26). Unsecured loans ₹4,613.59 million repayable on demand. Restrictive covenants in financing agreements. Trade receivables ₹13,749.57 million (59.11% of revenue). Net working capital ₹10,206.62 million. EBITDA margins improving but absolute debt levels rising significantly (FY24: ₹3,937.49 million → FY26: ₹8,282.34 million).

Promoters hold majority post-Offer; average acquisition cost ₹0.01 to Nil. Multiple complex restructurings and untraceable historical allotment records. Audit reports contain emphasis of matter for three consecutive years. Board has 3 independent directors out of 6. Promoter Deepak Goel has no formal education; Promoter Rakhi Goel has no professional experience beyond being a promoter. High number of other directorships for executive directors (Devesh Goel: 13, Akshat Goel: 12). No succession plan. KMP attrition: Whole-time Director Navin Kumar Saffar resigned June 30, 2025.

Installed capacity 85,448 MT but utilization only 61.59% (FY26). EPC bid-to-win ratio low (16.42% FY26). High dependence on contract labour (2,170 on third-party payroll FY26). Attrition 18.25% (FY26). All plants in West Bengal (concentration risk). Backward integration and TS Conductor partnership support scalability, but under-utilization and regional concentration limit operational flexibility.

Positioned as one of the leading players in East India for power cables and conductors. Strategic partnership with TS Conductor Corp for advanced conductors provides differentiation. Marquee government customer base (65.16% of revenue FY26). However, intense competition from larger national players (Polycab, KEI, Apar Industries) with significantly higher revenues and profitability. No disclosed market share percentage. Export revenue declining (4.17% FY24 → 2.19% FY26).

Multiple internal operational risks identified: customer concentration, supplier concentration, raw material price volatility, EPC execution risks, labour dependency, IT system vulnerability, insufficient insurance (18.04% assets uninsured FY26). Audit emphasis of matter for three years. Contingent liabilities ₹267.83 million (FY26). Historical corporate records not traceable. No past non-compliance table provided in extracted sections. Late delivery deductions indicate execution challenges.

red_flags: Audit reports for three consecutive fiscals (FY24, FY25, FY26) contain emphasis of matter on outstanding title deeds, working capital statement differences to banks, related-party loans/guarantees, and disputed statutory dues — indicating persistent governance/accounting concerns.

Promoter average cost of acquisition is ₹0.01 to Nil per share, while Offer Price is to be determined through book-building; combined with 8:1 bonus issue within 18 months of DRHP, raises significant dilution and promoter exit concerns.

Capacity utilization dropped to 61.59% in FY26 while installed capacity was expanded by ~37.82% over two years — suggests either aggressive capacity build-up ahead of demand or demand contraction.
Top 10 customers contributed 72.14% of revenue in FY26 with single largest customer at 24.82%; combined with government entity payment delays and state DISCOM indebtedness, receivables risk is acute.
No succession plan despite high dependence on Key Managerial Personnel and 18.25% attrition rate; Whole-time Director resigned in June 2025.
